x.text:
The midterm election delivered a considerably stronger Democratic showing than the market was anticipating. Democrats captured both the House and Senate, with gains extending well beyond the traditional battlegrounds and into states and districts that had been reliably Republican. The result is a genuine blue wave and, from the market's perspective, the important issue this morning isn't politics -- it's surprise. Markets can discount good news and bad news; what they have a more difficult time discounting is an outcome that wasn't fully anticipated.

Historically, that reduction in legislative flexibility has not necessarily been a negative for stocks. Markets generally prefer predictability, and divided government can make sweeping changes in taxes, spending and regulation more difficult to enact. Fidelity's research makes an important point: historically, the market's post-election behavior has been driven less by which political party won than by the reduction in uncertainty once the election was over. As Fidelity puts it, the environment doesn't necessarily become completely clear - it simply becomes “less unclear.” And this is where the historical picture becomes particularly interesting.

Since 1938, the S&P 500 has been higher 95% of the time during the 12 months following a midterm election, with an average gain of approximately 14%. Fidelity's longer-term work on the presidential cycle also shows the post-midterm year as historically the strongest portion of the four-year election cycle. Schwab finds a similar pattern: since 1974, the S&P 500 has averaged a 5.7% gain in the three months following midterms and 12.4% over the following six months.

That historical tendency is reinforced by seasonality. We have now entered what has traditionally been the strongest six-month period of the year, November through April. Since 1945, the S&P 500 has averaged roughly 7% during that six-month stretch versus just over 2% from May through October. November itself has historically been one of the market's strongest months, and the November through January period has also been particularly favorable

So we now have several potentially favorable historical forces beginning to converge: the election is behind us, political uncertainty has been reduced, Washington is moving toward divided government, we're entering the historically strongest part of the presidential cycle, and we're simultaneously moving into one of the strongest seasonal periods of the year.

That does not mean the market has to go straight up from here. In fact, given the magnitude of the election surprise, some additional volatility would not be unusual. The market still has to digest what the Democratic Congress could mean for taxes, regulation, AI infrastructure, energy policy and other areas. More importantly, the election doesn't make the other risks disappear. The 10-year Treasury yield remains near 5%, oil remains above $100, inflation and Fed policy remain significant issues, and questions surrounding AI valuations and capital spending are still very much in play. Those fundamental forces ultimately matter more than the election itself.

What matters now is whether the tape begins to confirm the historical script. I want to see the major indexes absorb the election shock and hold support, but even more important, I want to see improvement beneath the surface: broader participation, expanding leadership, more stocks reclaiming key moving averages, fewer new lows, more quality setups and, ultimately, breakouts that can gain traction and hold their gains.

Encouragingly, breadth has already improved, with nearly two-thirds of S&P 500 stocks moving above their 10-week averages after starting the month at only about 20%.

The bottom line is that the election result may have been more dramatic than investors expected, and the market's initial volatility reflects that surprise. But the election also removes a major uncertainty, creates divided government and places us directly into a historically favorable post-midterm and seasonal window. If the market needs to shake out further in the near term, I would not automatically interpret that as bearish. It could be part of the process of discounting the new political reality and establishing a more durable low.

Of course, the historical and seasonal backdrop doesn't guarantee the outcome. Stock setups will be our main focus. In the meantime, our shorts act as a hedge, and as always, our longs are protected with stops.

1) 🛢️  IRAN - PEACE DOESN'T REBUILD WHAT THE WAR DESTROYED

- 🇮🇷 Iran says it has consulted 12 countries over the past 48 hours
- 🇶🇦 Qatar confirms mediation is continuing
- 🇺🇸 Trump says negotiations are progressing, despite continued limited American strikes

🤝 For investors, this is an improvement in diplomatic activity - not yet an agreement

🔍 But there's a bigger issue that almost disappears from the headlines
🚨 WHAT HAPPENS AFTER A DEAL IS SIGNED?

🇶🇦 Look at Qatar
💥 Iranian strikes damaged two LNG production units at QatarEnergy's Ras Laffan facility
⚡ Those units represent approximately 17% of Qatar's LNG export capacity

📊 QatarEnergy estimates:
🏗️ Around THREE YEARS to repair them
💸 Approximately $20 BILLION in lost revenue per year

⚠️ Even if peace is signed tomorrow, 
the damaged capacity doesn't return tomorrow
🏭 Qatar could restart unaffected production much faster — provided ships are available — but its total output would remain below pre-war capacity while repairs continue

🔗 And the problem doesn't end at the processing plant
- ⚓ Tankers need to return
- 🛡️ Shipowners need confidence that routes are safe
- 📜 Insurers need to be willing to cover voyages at commercially viable prices
- 🚢 Ports and shipping schedules must absorb months of disruption

💰 During the conflict, insurance and transit expenses rose dramatically
🚢Some tanker passages became prohibitively expensive

🚨 A CEASEFIRE CAN REDUCE THE PRICE OF RISK IMMEDIATELY
🚫IT CANNOT REMOVE THE COST OF PHYSICAL DAMAGE

👀 Now look at what Qatar is doing about it
🇺🇸 The company has been purchasing long-term LNG supplies from the United States and other producers

🔄 This isn't simply about replacing missing gas today
🛡️ It's also a strategy to protect its trading business against future disruptions to Hormuz

🌍 And the shift is broader than Iran
🇹🇷 Turkey says it is reducing purchases of Russian gas because American alternatives are more competitive on price — while making clear it isn't abandoning Russian supply entirely

💡 That's an important development
🇪🇺 Europe's restrictions on Russian energy remain a separate obstacle, and Russia's access to other customers still depends on commercial terms

⚠️ So even after the fighting stops, the pre-war energy system won't automatically reassemble itself

📜 New contracts have been signed
🚢 Routes have changed
🏗️ Infrastructure needs repair
🔄 Buyers have found alternatives

💰 WHERE DOES THE MONEY GO?
🏗️ To replacement supplies, repairs, shipping, insurance, storage and infrastructure that reduces dependence on vulnerable routes

📉 Some producers may receive lower commodity prices after peace
📈 But companies providing reliable deliveries and rebuilding damaged capacity could continue receiving investment for years

🎯 THE WAR CAN END BEFORE THE ENERGY BILL DOES

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
2) 🇺🇦 UKRAINE - TRUMP IS NEGOTIATING PEACE, BUT THE ORDER OF THE AGREEMENT IS NOW THE PROBLEM

🇺🇸 Trump continues describing a possible large agreement involving Ukraine and European security
🤝 Russia, Ukraine and the US are preparing for negotiations in Abu Dhabi on November 10

⚠️ But the latest statements expose a fundamental disagreement
- 🇺🇦 Ukraine and European governments want an end to the fighting to be the immediate priority
- 🇪🇺 EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas insists that Europe must participate in decisions concerning European security
- 🛡️ She has also rejected the idea that Russia should determine NATO's or the EU's future security arrangements
- 🇷🇺 Moscow has its own demands concerning regional security

🚨 THIS IS NO LONGER JUST A QUESTION OF WHETHER EVERYONE WANTS THE WAR TO END
⚖️ It's about what must be agreed BEFORE the war can end - and what can be negotiated AFTERWARD

💡 That distinction matters
🕊️ A ceasefire is a commitment to stop fighting
🤝 A lasting settlement needs arrangements that make renewed fighting less likely

💰 And those arrangements require money
- 🛡️ Who finances Ukraine's long-term defense?
- 🏦 Who provides credible security guarantees?
- 🏗️ Who pays for reconstruction?
- ⚡ What happens to damaged energy infrastructure?
- 📜 Which sanctions remain, and under what conditions could they be lifted?

⚠️ Even if military operations stop, security expenses don't disappear:
- 🇺🇦 Ukraine still needs reconstruction
- 🇪🇺European governments still need defense budgets 
- 💵Investors still need legal certainty before committing long-term capital

📈 That's why a peace announcement can lift market sentiment without immediately changing the financing needs of the countries involved

🤝 The negotiations in Abu Dhabi may produce important progress
🎯 But the test is whether the parties can agree on obligations that can actually be implemented 
- not simply announce that progress has been made

🎯 PEACE CAN CHANGE THE POLITICAL OUTLOOK IN A DAY
💰 REBUILDING SECURITY AND ECONOMIC CONFIDENCE TAKES LONGER

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
3) 🤖 AI - THE BIGGEST RISK ISN'T WHETHER THE TECHNOLOGY WORKS
🚨 A $500 MILLION LOAN SALE MAY TELL US MORE THAN ANOTHER $50 BILLION IN AI PROMISES

🏦 Dutch bank ING is reportedly offering a portfolio of approximately $500 million in data-centre loans
📋 The portfolio includes 12 loans, with some exposure connected to the Stargate AI infrastructure initiative
📅 Buyers have been invited to submit bids by November 19

⚠️ A bank selling loans isn't automatically evidence that borrowers are in trouble

🔍 But it creates an important test:
💰 WHAT PRICE WILL OTHER INVESTORS PAY TO TAKE ON THAT RISK?

📉 If buyers demand substantial discounts, that could indicate the market now requires higher returns to finance certain AI projects

👀 And there's a second development
🇺🇸 Microsoft is reportedly winding down an agreement to rent AI computing capacity from Oracle
🤖 The reason isn't that Microsoft no longer needs AI
💾 The rented infrastructure used older Nvidia chips and no longer matched Microsoft's evolving requirements

🧠 Now think about the business model
- 🏗️ A company spends billions building a data centre
- 💸 It buys hardware and finances construction
- 📈 It expects customers to rent the computing capacity for years
⚡ But AI hardware improves rapidly

⚠️ If customers begin demanding newer technology before earlier infrastructure earns back its cost, the operator faces a difficult question:
🚨 HOW LONG WILL TODAY'S EXPENSIVE EQUIPMENT GENERATE ENOUGH REVENUE TO REPAY YESTERDAY'S DEBT?

🎯 That's the risk
❌ Not that AI is useless
❌ Not that every data centre will fail
⏳ But that technology can advance faster than some investments recover their cost

💰 Meanwhile, OpenAI has secured another approximately $11 billion in funding

✅ Clearly, investors haven't abandoned AI
⚖️ They're making distinctions:
- 🚀 One company attracts fresh capital
- 🏦 Another sells debt
- 🔄 A third changes its computing contracts

💡 Those decisions may all be rational 
- because these businesses have different customers, costs and obligations

🔍 The next important evidence isn't another AI valuation headline
📊 It's the price investors offer for existing AI loans, the durability of customer contracts and the cash flow the infrastructure actually generates

🎯 THE REAL AI QUESTION IS NO LONGER JUST HOW BIG THE INDUSTRY CAN BECOME
💵 IT'S WHO WILL EARN ENOUGH TO REPAY THE COST OF BUILDING IT

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
4) 🏦 THE US JOBS REPORT 
- GOOD FOR WORKERS, COMPLICATED FOR INVESTORS

🇺🇸 The October employment report delivered a clear surprise
💼 Jobs created: +165,000
📊 Expected: approximately +65,000
📉 Unemployment: 4.1%, down from 4.2%

📈 The previous two months were also revised higher
🇺🇸 That's evidence of a more resilient American labor market than economists expected

👀 But the market's response is where things become interesting
🏦 The stronger report increased expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise rates again in December

📊 US Treasury yields rose, and the dollar strengthened

🤔 Why?
💼 Because an economy that's still creating jobs gives the Fed less reason to support growth with cheaper credit
🔥 And with inflation already elevated, policymakers have another reason to remain cautious

💡 Now here's the important distinction
🚨 A STRONG ECONOMY DOESN'T REQUIRE A STRONG STOCK MARKET AT EVERY PRICE

- 📈 A company can be growing while its shares are too expensive
- ⚖️ Investors value not only future profits, but also how much those profits are worth today compared with the returns available elsewhere
- 📜 Higher bond yields make some future profits less attractive at existing stock valuations
- 🛡️ Yet strong employment also reduces immediate fears of recession

📈 That's why the Nasdaq could rebound 1.1% 
on Friday even as expectations of another rate increase strengthened
- ⚠️ The rebound doesn't prove the selling is over
- 📉 The Nasdaq still finished the week down 3.4%

👥 And retail investors weren't simply buying every decline

💸 Vanda Research recorded unusually heavy retail selling during Thursday's collapse, even though some buyers returned later

🔍 That matters for our previous discussion about who is buying
⚖️ We cannot assume that every market recovery is funded by retail optimism or that every decline means institutional investors are moving into bonds

📊 We need the actual flows

🎯 THE MARKET ISN'T JUST ASKING WHETHER AMERICANS STILL HAVE JOBS
💰 It's asking whether corporate earnings can grow enough to justify valuations while financing remains expensive

🔄 And that brings us back to the asset we've been questioning since August

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
5) 🟠 BITCOIN - WE FINALLY HAVE MORE THAN 
A PRICE CHART TO EXAMINE

📅 November 5:
🟠 Bitcoin recovered above $80,000
🔍 We questioned whether the rebound had enough new buyers behind it

📅 November 6:
📉 BTC fell below $75,000 before recovering somewhat

👀 And now there's an important piece of evidence
🏦 US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $430 million in net outflows on November 5

📊 That was after a relatively small net inflow on November 4
⚠️ This doesn't prove that all investors are abandoning Bitcoin

🔄 ETF activity is only one part of the market

💸 But it does show that a major channel of investment demand was experiencing net withdrawals during the same period that the price recovery was losing strength

💡 That's much more useful than simply saying the chart looks bearish

🤔 Here's why:
⚖️ When sellers enter a market, the outcome depends partly on how much buying demand is waiting

🌊 In a deep market, substantial selling can be absorbed without an enormous price move
📉 In a thin market, selling can push prices down much faster

⚠️ If traders have also borrowed heavily to buy Bitcoin, falling prices may force them to close positions
💥 That creates additional selling

🔻 And if the market is still struggling to attract sustained spot demand, a temporary recovery can quickly reverse

🚨 THIS IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A PRICE REBOUND AND A CHANGE IN THE UNDERLYING BUYING TREND

🎯 Our August warning wasn't that Bitcoin could never rise
🔍 It was that sharp recoveries should not automatically be interpreted as proof that a fresh, durable wave of buyers has arrived

⚠️ The recent ETF withdrawals strengthen the case for caution

📊 But we still need to watch whether flows reverse, whether market depth improves and whether buying continues after leverage is reduced

🎯 THE NEXT IMPORTANT BITCOIN SIGNAL ISN'T ANOTHER GREEN CANDLE
💰 IT'S WHETHER REAL BUYERS CONTINUE SHOWING UP WHEN THE SELLERS RETURN

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
6) ✴️ MEXC - THE EXCHANGE IS OPERATING, BUT ITS ACCESS TO THE FINANCIAL SYSTEM IS UNDER THREAT

🇺🇸 On November 6, the US Treasury announced an order restricting financial transfers involving MEXC Global
⚖️ FinCEN alleges that the exchange facilitated at least $16 billion in illicit transactions connected to sanctions evasion and other activities

👀 Now MEXC has responded
🛡️ The company says trading continues normally, customer assets remain secure and it intends to cooperate with regulators

🔍 Those statements don't necessarily contradict the US action

🚨 AN EXCHANGE CAN HOLD CUSTOMER ASSETS AND KEEP TRADING WHILE LOSING ACCESS TO IMPORTANT BANKING CHANNELS

🏦 The US order targets transfers involving American financial institutions

🌍 It does not automatically mean every customer account worldwide has been frozen

⚠️ Nor does MEXC's assurance that customer funds are safe remove the legal restrictions

📅 The order is scheduled to take effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register

🤔 Why should investors care?
🔗 Because crypto exchanges are businesses connected to both blockchains and the traditional financial system

💳 They need payment providers, banking partners, liquidity providers and counterparties willing to deal with them

💸 If those relationships weaken, a platform can face rising costs and reduced commercial flexibility even while its trading engine continues operating

⚖️ This is a business and regulatory risk 
- not proof of an immediate customer-asset loss

🔎 The next thing to watch is whether MEXC can preserve its operational relationships and respond effectively to the regulatory action

🎯 BLOCKCHAIN TRANSACTIONS CAN BE DECENTRALIZED
🏛️ THE BUSINESSES CONNECTING THEM TO THE FINANCIAL SYSTEM STILL FACE REAL-WORLD CONSTRAINTS

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🏁 THE REAL LESSON OF NOVEMBER 7

🌍 This week brought several very different developments
- 🇮🇷 Iran intensified diplomacy
- 🏦 AI lenders began testing the market for existing debt
- 🇺🇸 The US labor market proved stronger than expected
- 🟠 Bitcoin's recovery faced renewed selling
- ⚖️ And a major crypto exchange faced restrictions on access to US finance

🔍 These events aren't all caused by the same thing
💡 But they reveal an important distinction between what markets expect and what economies can actually deliver

🛢️ A peace agreement can change oil futures immediately
🏗️Damaged energy facilities still need years of repair

🇺🇦 A diplomatic announcement can change expectations
🛡️Security guarantees still need financing and enforcement

🤖 An AI company can raise billions
💵Its infrastructure still needs customers and sufficient revenue to repay its costs

🇺🇸 A strong economy can lift corporate earnings
💵Expensive financing can still pressure stock valuations

🟠 Bitcoin can rally
⚠️A sustainable advance still requires sufficient buying demand

✴️ A crypto exchange can keep operating
🏦Its access to banking infrastructure can still deteriorate

🚨 THE MARKET PRICES WHAT IT EXPECTS TO HAPPEN
💰 CAPITAL EVENTUALLY HAS TO PAY FOR WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS

🎯 And that's the gap we're watching
🔎 Not just who promises the next great opportunity

⚖️ But who is building something necessary, who is paying for it, who is receiving the revenue 
- and who is left carrying the risk

🙉 SURVIVE FIRST
🙈 PROFIT LATER
🎯 FOLLOW THE CAPITAL

Ten million people have watched a University of Chicago professor accidentally destroy the entire online writing course industry.

Online writing cohorts charge $4,000 for six weeks of templates. A Chicago writing director delivered the whole counter-argument in 80 minutes for free.

His name is Larry McEnerney. He is the director of the University of Chicago Writing Program and the professor who has spent 40 years telling PhDs and faculty that everything they learned about writing in school is actively hurting their work.

For four decades he has opened the same lecture with the same line. Nobody outside school is paid to care about you or what is in your head.

His entire framework fits on a napkin.

Rules are for cheap memos, not valuable writing. Clear and useless is still useless. Organized and useless is still useless. Persuasive and useless is still useless. Value is not in your head and value is not in the world. Value is what a specific community of readers has decided is valuable. Writing does not transfer your ideas. It changes theirs.

That last rule alone has probably cost the online writing industry a hundred million dollars in dropped-out cohorts.

"Nobody outside school is paid to care about you."

That is McEnerney on his own stage, 40 years into watching faculty write papers nobody will read. He was not exaggerating.

Executives pay $4,000 for a six-week writing cohort and still open every memo with their own biography. Founders ship a 2,000-word essay every Monday and never once ask whether anyone in their community has a problem it actually solves.

The lecture is free on YouTube. McEnerney's handouts have been posted at the UChicago Writing Program site for over a decade.

McEnerney still runs the program in Chicago. Almost none of the ten million viewers have spent 15 minutes today reading their field for code-words, the exercise he actually prescribed.

The method is free. The willingness to actually write for someone other than yourself is the entire edge.

Tony Robbins charges $5,000 for a weekend seminar on self-belief. A university soccer coach delivered the whole method in 13 minutes for free.

His name is Dr. Ivan Joseph. He is a two-time national championship soccer coach, former Athletics Director at Ryerson University, and one of the few people who publicly argues that self-confidence is a skill that can be trained, not a personality trait you are born with or without.

For over a decade he has opened every recruiting meeting with the same line to every parent. The one thing he actually looks for is not vision, not speed, not a great left foot. It is self-confidence.

His entire framework fits on a napkin.

Self-confidence is a skill, not a gift. Repetition is the only path: his Colombian goalie caught 350 balls a day for 8 months and now plays in Europe. Persistence beats talent, Edison took up to 10,000 tries and Rowling took 12 publishers before Harry Potter sold. Rewrite your self-talk because no one else will tell you you are the greatest. Catch people when they are good, including yourself, including a letter you wrote to yourself on a day you felt proud. Interpret feedback the way you choose to interpret it.

That last rule alone has probably cost the self-help industry a hundred million dollars in unfinished mindset courses.

"I am the captain of my ship and the master of my fate."

That is Joseph on the TEDx stage, reading the affirmation he kept beside his mirror when he first took a job he was not sure he could do.

Founders spend $5,000 on mindset retreats and still freeze before every investor pitch. Parents sign their kid up for a confidence camp and never let the kid fail at the same drill 350 times in a row.

The talk is free on YouTube. Joseph's book "You Got This" is under twenty dollars on Amazon.

Joseph still runs leadership programs in Canada. Almost none of the ten million viewers have written themselves the self-confidence letter he described.

The method is free. The willingness to actually repeat the thing you keep avoiding is the entire edge.

Oil has fed more strongly into core inflation since the pandemic, according to this paper from Fed researchers.

But has inflation’s behavior changed? Or have supply shocks become more frequent or persistent?

The answer matters for how forcefully central banks should respond.

x.name: Nick Timiraos
x.text:
"With no post-pandemic dynamics (the black line), core inflation edges up only modestly, peaking near 2.2%.

Allowing for stronger persistence (the red line) raises the path to a plateau of about 2.5%. 

Adding stronger pass-through from oil prices as well (the blue line) produces the highest and most front-loaded response: core inflation climbs to nearly 2.8% around mid-2027, roughly 0.6 pp above the path implied by pre-pandemic dynamics, before receding toward about 2.2% by the end of 2028."

x.name: Peter Schiff
x.text:
Last year, the Trustee appointed by OCIF alleged that Brent de Jong of Qenta was trying to steal $50 million from Euro Pacific Bank customers. I believe the actual amount is higher. But instead of filing an action aimed at recovering those funds, the Trustee filed a RICO lawsuit that falsely accused me of conspiring with de Jong. I believe he named me to smear me, even though I was the only one trying to get customers’ money back.

I believe the RICO lawsuit would have been dismissed. The Trustee ultimately settled with Qenta and voluntarily dismissed the case with prejudice. As part of the settlement, he released de Jong from all the claims he had asserted against him in the lawsuit, even though I believe de Jong was trying to steal customers’ money. I was not a party to the settlement, but the dismissal with prejudice applied to me as well.

It’s now been more than six months since the Trustee dismissed the lawsuit. Qenta is clearly in breach of the settlement, yet the Trustee has taken no action to enforce it. For example, Qenta agreed to pay all claims related to the bank’s mutual funds that are currently under its control, yet in over six months not one penny has been paid. Had I been given control of those funds, I would have returned them all in less than two weeks.

The Trustee is also in breach of his own agreement because he was required to demand that Qenta make up a $41 million shortfall to pay claims of customers who returned to the bank through reverse migration. Yet, to my knowledge, the Trustee has demanded that Qenta return only about $10 million of what is owed. My guess is that he hasn’t asked for the rest because he knows Qenta won’t pay and he doesn’t want to sue Qenta for breach.

During those six months, I’ve repeatedly urged the Trustee to take legal action against Qenta. I also asked him to authorize me to pursue recovery and offered to pay the legal costs out of my own pocket so the bank’s estate wouldn’t bear the expense. He has refused to act or to authorize me to pursue recovery in his place.

비트코인 채굴은 거대 채굴 회사만의 판이라는 말, 하루에 두 번이나 빗나갔음.
개인 채굴자 두 명이 각각 블록 하나씩을 캐서 3.1BTC 넘게, 23만 달러 넘게 받았음.

블록을 누가 캘지는 미리 정해져 있지 않음. 계산을 돌린 쪽 중 조건을 먼저 맞춘 쪽이 가져감.
큰 채굴 회사는 확률이 높을 뿐이고, 작은 채굴자 몫의 확률도 0이 아님.

그 몫은 누구 허락으로 받는 게 아님. 규칙대로 계산했다는 증명 하나면 됨. 계좌 심사도, 신원 확인도 없음.

다만 이건 드문 결과임. 대부분의 개인 채굴자는 오랫동안 블록 하나도 못 캠. 
봐야 할 건 수익이 아니라 규칙임. 같은 규칙이 거대 회사와 개인에게 똑같이 적용됨.

비트코인은 이미 큰손들 판이라고 생각하는 당신, 오늘 블록 두 개는 규칙이 몸집을 따지지 않는다는 기록임.

x.text:
저는 비트마인을 전량 매도 후 TQQQ로 넘어가게 될 수도 있습니다. 혹시나 놀라실까봐 미리 말씀드리겠습니다..

사실 제가 이더리움 트레저리 기업인 BMNR을 
양가부모님에게 약 2천만원씩 8천만원, 
평단 $47 에 305주씩 증여드린 것까지도 
아시는 분들은 아시겠지만 확신을 했었고,
이더리움과 비트마인에 대한 그 확신은 지금도 변함이 없습니다. 

다만, 저는 마음 속에 1가지 의문은 계속 남게 되었습니다.
제 메인글과 메인글의 인용글을 보신 분들은 아시겠지만
저는 지금도 여전히 미국지수 ETF 레버리지를 사라고 외치고 있습니다.

왜 그럴까.. 지금 이 상황에서 내가 원하는 것이 무엇일까..
네.. 잠도 못자고 깊은 고민을 하다가 깨달았습니다.
결국 저의 최종 목적지는 결국 QLD·TQQQ 둘 중 하나라는 것을..

개별종목보다 지수 ETF 레버리지를 왜 찬양하게 되었고 그 확신이 점점 커질 수 밖에 없었는지..
사실 이유는 2가지 정도로 압축해볼 수 있을 것 같습니다.

첫 번째는, 암호화폐가 과연 언제 갈 것인가?
가격만 너무 보는 거 아니냐고 하실 수도 있는데 맞습니다.
가치만 믿고 기다리기에는 저는 외벌이 가장이고,
생활비가 ~28년 6월까지 정해져 있습니다.
사실 미국주식 시가총액 합에 비하면, 암호화폐는 코스피보다도 못해서 저는 잘 따라갈 것이라 생각했는데 트럼프가와 정치적으로 엮이면서 계속 나스닥과 디커플링이 되더라구요.
결국 가격은 가치에 수렴할 것이라는 것은 변함없으나,
저는 계속 이러한 상황이 지속된다면..? 하는 두려움이 계속 마음 속에 있었던 것 같습니다. 

두 번째는, 반도체와 나스닥의 디커플링입니다.
사실 최근에 SOXL이라는 반도체 3배 레버리지는 폭락을 하는 반면, TQQQ는 반등하여 올랐던 것을 보고 또 느꼈습니다.
또 디커플링이 일어나더라구요?
사실 지수 ETF와 반대로 가는 것이 나쁜 것만은 아닐 겁니다.
지수 ETF는 떨어지는 것과 반대로 오르는 날도 있겠죠.

그러나 제가 이 날들에서 느꼈던 것은 
아.. 결국 암호화폐도 반도체도 하나의 섹터다.
하나의 섹터라 함은 이것들을 개별종목의 일부라고 봐야겠다.
결국 이 모든 것의 합은 지수 ETF이고, 나는 처음부터 개별종목이 아닌 지수 ETF를 원했구나..  
라는 생각이 너무나도 강하게 들었습니다.

어쩌면 제가 메인글과 메인글의 인용에서 외쳤던 것은
제 스스로에게 너가 정한 원칙으로 투자를 하고 있었던 게 맞냐고 물었던 것 같습니다..

사실 제가 개별종목인 비트마인을 투자했던 이유는 단순합니다.
확실한 지수 ETF가 아닌, 내가 공부하고 종목을 발굴하여 장기투자하는 멋진 꿈을 꾸고 있었던 것 같습니다.

그러나, 저는 그렇기에는 너무 쫄보고 유리심장이라고 생각이 들었습니다. 이더리움과 비트마인의 미래를 믿습니다.
다만, 제가 그것보다 지수 ETF의 위대함을 본능적으로 따라가고 싶다는 생각을 하고 있었던 것 같습니다.

그런 취지로 이 글을 적게 되었구요.. 
오늘 아내가 일어나면 진지하게 얘기해볼 생각입니다.
자, 그래서 왜 TQQQ냐..
저는 25년생인 딸아이에게는 QLD를 증여했습니다.  

저는 QLD 베타값이 엔비디아 정도여서, 
딸아이에게 바랬던 것은 다음과 같았던 것 같습니다. 
"최소한 주식을 하려면 엔비디아 정도의 변동성 버텨야 하지 않나?"

네.. 그런데 저 개인적으로는 TQQQ를 더 좋아합니다.
제가 미국주식 처음 시작했던 것도 TQQQ였구요.
결국 QLD·TQQQ 둘 다 사랑하지만, 저 개인적인 마음의 기울기가 그렇습니다..

자, 알겠고..
굴렁쇠 너는 무슨 논리로 지금 시점에서 TQQQ로 넘어가게 될 수도 있다는 거냐?
네.. 메인글과 메인의 인용글을 꼭 보시고 지금 글을 봐주시길 부탁드리겠습니다. 
그 2개는 무조건 숙지하셔야 더 와닿으실 것 같습니다.

먼저 2017년~2026년 약 10년의 기간동안
제가 생각하는 최악의 하락장은 22년도 러vs우 전쟁입니다.
그리고 제가 지금 이 글에서 말씀드리는 것의 모든 기준은
현재 주봉 RSI가 35~36 사이이구요. 
그 시점을 기준으로 TQQQ의 가격과 방향성은 어땠는지를 간략히 보여드리는 겁니다.

먼저 1번 이미지를 보시면, 22년도에 주봉 RSI 36 구간에서 약 22개월의 하락장이 지속되었습니다.

2번 이미지를 보시면, 주봉 RSI 36에서 최저점까지 약 10개월이 걸렸습니다.
근데 저는 이것을 기준으로 투자를 하지 않으려고 합니다.

3번 이미지를 봐주시기 바랍니다. 
25년 4월, 26년 3월 모두 주봉 RSI 36 부근에서 3개월 이내 반등을 보여주었습니다. 
제가 이 글에서 반등이라 표현하는 것은, 내가 매수한 시점의 가격 이상을 말씀드리는 것입니다.

4번 이미지를 봐주시기 바랍니다.
제가 차트에 빨간색 동그라미 친 구간이 정확히 주봉 RSI 36 구간의 코로나 때 입니다.
이 때가 20년도 3월이죠.
이 구간에서 3개월 이내 반등합니다.

이미지가 최대 4장이라 너무 불편한 X..
사실 2018년도 미·중 무역 전쟁 때도 그랬습니다. 
트럼프 1기죠?

Earlier today I wrote that school destroys critical thinking. Many of you asked for proof.

The proof is Marx.

Marxism is probably the most tested theory in human history. Tested on paper by the best economists in the world. Tested at full scale on hundreds of millions of people, across several continents, for more than a century. And it failed every single test.

A free mind, one that checks its ideas against reality, cannot remain Marxist. If so many people still are, it's not a problem of intelligence. It's a problem of method. They were never taught to verify.

Let's start from the beginning.

In 1867, Marx publishes Das Kapital. Everything rests on one idea: the value of a good comes from the amount of labor it contains. The boss's profit is therefore labor stolen from the worker.

Four years later, in 1871, Menger and Jevons independently show that this is wrong. Value doesn't come from labor. It comes from the usefulness the buyer sees in the good. An hour spent digging a useless hole creates zero value. That's the marginal revolution, and all of modern economics is built on it.

In 1896, Böhm-Bawerk shows that Marx's system contradicts itself: real prices don't match labor values, and Marx knew it. The foundation collapses.

In 1920, Mises asks the question that kills it: without private property, there are no market prices. Without prices, how does a central planner know what to produce, how much, and with which resources? Answer: he can't. Hayek finishes the job in 1945: economic knowledge is scattered across millions of minds, and no central bureau can ever gather it.

That's the theory. Now the predictions.

Marx predicted the revolution would break out in the most industrialized countries, England and Germany. It happened in Russia, an agrarian country. Wrong.

He predicted workers would grow poorer and poorer under capitalism. They grew richer than at any point in history. Wrong.

He predicted the State would wither away. Everywhere his ideas were applied, the State became total. Wrong.

Now the experiments.

USSR: forced collectivization, famine in Ukraine, millions dead, the Gulag.

China: Mao's Great Leap Forward. Between 15 and 45 million dead depending on the historian. The largest famine in human history, produced by a plan.

Cambodia: the Khmer Rouge killed roughly a quarter of their own population in four years.

Then there are the natural experiments. The most brutal ones, because they eliminate every excuse.

Korea. Same people, same language, same culture, same history. In 1945, the North was richer than the South. Today, income per person in the South is about 29 times higher than in the North. Only one variable changed: the system.

Germany. One people cut in two. One side had to build a wall. Not to keep people out. To keep them in.

Venezuela. The largest proven oil reserves on the planet. Nearly 8 million people fled the country. 21st-century socialism ended with Maduro captured last January.

Meanwhile, the other system, the one you were taught to hate, did this: in 1820, about three quarters of humanity lived in extreme poverty. Today, around 10%. And the biggest escape from poverty in history, China after 1978, happened at the exact moment the Communist Party brought markets back.

From Marx to Maduro, 150 years of data. All pointing the same way.

So how does anyone stay Marxist?

With the magic sentence: "that wasn't real communism."

Think about what that sentence means. A theory that fails every time it's tried, whose believers then declare that none of the attempts counted, is no longer a theory. It's a faith. Karl Popper saw it as early as 1945: Marxism survived its refutations by making itself irrefutable.

A mind trained to think for itself asks one question: how many failures does it take before you question the hypothesis? One, two, ten, forty?

That's exactly the question school never teaches you to ask.

Marx isn't taught as a hypothesis to test against the data. He's taught as a morality tale: there are oppressors and oppressed, and the right side is obvious. You learn the conclusion, never the method.

A four-year-old would ask: "Okay, but where did it work?" Fifteen years of schooling later, they've stopped asking.

A system that teaches you to obey has no interest in teaching you to verify. Because the day you start verifying is the day you start being free.

And that day, you stop being a Marxist.

x.name: Brivael Le Pogam
x.text:
A few years ago, Peter Thiel wrote to Mark Zuckerberg: 70% of Millennials say they're pro-socialist.

His conclusion: stop calling them stupid, and try to understand why.

His explanation was economic. Too much student debt, unaffordable housing, no capital. When you own nothing, you have no reason to defend the system.

He's right. But that's only half the story.

The other half is school.

School destroys critical thinking. Methodically. For fifteen years.

You learn to recite instead of question. To find the expected answer instead of the true one. To obey authority instead of reasoning for yourself.

When you've spent your youth outsourcing your thinking to an institution, it feels natural to outsource your life to an even bigger one: the State.

That's why so many end up Marxist. Not by conviction. By conditioning.

And that conditioning is about to become a handicap.

We're entering a world where AI does everything conformist, predictable and standardized better than we do. The only value left is thinking differently.

To create value tomorrow, you'll need to be neurodivergent.

And someone who thinks differently and reasons from first principles almost always ends up seeing the same thing: the State, as it works today, destroys more value than it creates.

It's no accident that Alex Karp created a fellowship at Palantir dedicated to neurodivergent talent. To him, in the age of AI, there are only two ways to have a future: master a real trade, or be neurodivergent.

But I'll go further than Karp.

I believe neurodivergence isn't the exception. It's the natural state of the human mind.

Look at a four-year-old. They ask hundreds of questions a day. They take everything apart. They refuse any rule they don't understand. They think from first principles without even knowing it's a thing.

Then they go to school. And we spend fifteen years normalizing them.

School doesn't shape minds. It sands them down.

The future belongs to those who survived the sanding.

x.name: Brivael Le Pogam
x.text:
If students are cheating on exams, stop treating them like criminals. Treat it as a signal.

An exam that an AI can pass for you doesn't measure your intelligence. It measures exactly what the machine already does: recite, apply, return the expected answer. When a student cheats with ChatGPT, he isn't gaming the test. He's proving the test no longer measures anything of value.

And that's where the problem gets dizzying.

For fifteen years, school trains our kids to do precisely what AI does better than them. Find the right answer instead of asking the right question. Follow the method instead of challenging it. Fit inside the grid instead of thinking outside it.

What it destroys along the way is the only thing that still makes us irreplaceable: divergent thinking and critical thinking. The ability to see the problem differently. To say "no, that doesn't hold up" when everyone else is nodding. To reason from first principles instead of repeating the consensus.

We are mass-producing humans optimized to be replaced.

But once again, someone thought through the alternative. And he didn't just talk about it.

In 2014, Elon Musk pulls his five kids out of their private school in Los Angeles. Not some neighborhood school: one of the most prestigious in the city, built for gifted children. He didn't think it was good enough. So he did what he always does. He built his own.

It's called Ad Astra, "to the stars." It sits right on the SpaceX campus in Hawthorne. He hires one of his kids' teachers, Josh Dahn, to design it. And he opens it to the children of SpaceX employees, for free. Around forty students at its peak.

What he said about school explains everything he built.

He said he hated school as a kid, that it felt like torture.

He said you should teach the problem, not the tools. His example became famous: if you want to teach a kid how an engine works, you don't give a lecture on screwdrivers and wrenches. You hand him an engine and tell him to take it apart. Then he understands why he needs the screwdriver. The tool becomes obvious because the problem is real.

He said sorting kids into grades by age is an assembly line. That some kids are great at math or languages and others aren't, and education should match each child's aptitude instead of moving everyone forward at the same pace.

So at Ad Astra, there are no age-based grades. No report cards. No foreign languages, because he believed real-time translation would make them obsolete. Instead: AI, robotics, coding, solving concrete problems. The kids build robots, run projects, defend their ideas in front of each other.

And above all, ethical dilemmas. "Conundrums." A town, a factory that employs everyone but pollutes the lake. What do you do? There's no answer key. You have to reason, argue, change your mind, persuade. The exact opposite of a multiple-choice test.

Musk even came in himself to teach the kids first principles thinking.

The school left the SpaceX campus in 2020, when his kids finished the program. But the team didn't disband. It became Astra Nova, an online school open to kids around the world, and spun off Synthesis, collaborative simulations where kids solve complex problems as a team. And today, Musk is relaunching an Ad Astra school in Texas, right next to the SpaceX, Starlink and Boring Company offices.

Think about the symbolism. The man who sends rockets into orbit and lands them back on Earth looked at the education system and concluded it had to start from zero. Not reform it. Rebuild it from first principles.

Students who cheat aren't the problem. They're the symptom. The problem is a system that trains humans to do what machines already do.

AI is making school as we know it obsolete. The only question is who will have the courage to build the next one.

x.name: Brivael Le Pogam
x.text:
The left wants you to stay dumb. And even if you went to an elite school, they got to you too.

Here's how it happened. Decision by decision. And the names of the people who tried to warn you.

It starts in Prussia. In 1807, after Napoleon crushed their army, Fichte delivers his Addresses to the German Nation. His thesis: the state must shape the child so completely that he can no longer want anything other than what the state wants. Prussia builds the first modern mass school system on that principle.

In 1843, Horace Mann visits Prussia and comes back in awe. In 1852, Massachusetts passes America's first compulsory schooling law. The model is imported almost intact: age cohorts, bells, standardized curriculum, obedience as the real lesson.

To be fair, at this stage it isn't the left. It's kings and industrialists. In 1913, Frederick Gates, who ran Rockefeller's General Education Board, wrote openly that they had no intention of turning rural children into philosophers or men of learning. They wanted workers.

So the machine was built to produce compliance. Then the progressive left took over the machine and did something worse. It kept the obedience and threw out the knowledge.

In 1918, William Kilpatrick, at Columbia's Teachers College, publishes The Project Method. Knowledge becomes secondary. What matters is the child's "experience." Teachers College goes on to train the people who train America's teachers.

In 1955, Rudolf Flesch publishes Why Johnny Can't Read. His point is simple: kids are no longer taught to turn letters into sounds. They're taught to memorize whole words by sight. It's a bestseller. The education establishment treats him as a crank.

In 1967, Ken Goodman publishes a paper describing reading as "a psycholinguistic guessing game." Literally. Out of it come whole language, then "balanced literacy," then three-cueing: a child stuck on a word is told to guess it from the picture.

From 1968 to 1977, the US government runs Project Follow Through, the largest education experiment in history. Around 200,000 kids, nearly a billion dollars, about twenty competing teaching models. One model wins in every category: Siegfried Engelmann's Direct Instruction. Explicit, structured, demanding. It even wins on self-esteem, the very thing the "child-centered" models claimed to protect.

The result? Buried. Schools of education, foundations and publishers attacked the data, and they won. The models that failed kept being promoted. Engelmann spent the rest of his life trying to get someone to listen. He died in 2019, still ignored by the institutions he had proven wrong.

In 1991, John Taylor Gatto, New York State Teacher of the Year, quits. He announces it in the Wall Street Journal: he no longer wants to hurt kids to make a living. In Dumbing Us Down, he lists what school actually teaches: confusion, your place in the hierarchy, indifference, emotional and intellectual dependency, self-worth that depends on outside approval. The system filed him under eccentric.

France, same story. In 2003, Rachel Boutonnet publishes the diary of a teacher who had to teach phonics in secret because her training institute pushed the global method. Marc Le Bris, Jean-Paul Brighelli with La Fabrique du crétin: all labeled reactionaries. Fifteen years later, neuroscience, led by Stanislas Dehaene, proved them right. Meanwhile French fourth graders finished last in the EU in math.

Back to America. Lucy Calkins, Teachers College again, sells her reading curriculum to about one elementary school in four. Three-cueing everywhere. It takes a journalist, Emily Hanford, and a podcast, Sold a Story, to blow it up in 2022. Calkins rewrites her curriculum. Dozens of states ban cueing. Sixty-seven years after Flesch.

The bill: in 2024, 12th grade reading hit the lowest score ever recorded by the Nation's Report Card. 40% of fourth graders are below the most basic level.

And the elite schools? "I went to a top school, this isn't about me." Wrong. Harvard's own 2025 report found about 60% of grades are now A's, versus roughly a quarter twenty years ago. When everyone gets an A, the grade no longer measures mastery. It measures conformity. The elite weren't spared the sanding. They just got finer sandpaper.

Look at the pattern. It's the same every time. An ideology replaces evidence. Whoever brings evidence is labeled a crank or a reactionary. Decades later, the system quietly corrects itself, nobody is held accountable, and a generation has been lost.

Expanding on why I believe "ETH as store of value (SoV)" makes much more sense to focus on than "ETH as fee-burning token".

Three primary reasons:

1. ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed
2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand Ethereum and ETH function in ways that are very hard to make compatible with decentralization and capture resistance.
3. Meanwhile, optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with Ethereum focusing on its unique strengths (decentralization and CROPS)

EIP-1559 (including its burn) is fine and good, we should keep them. But we should not feel sad if fee burn is < 10% of breakeven indefinitely; the value of ETH comes from elsewhere.

The core idea: the big thing that people appreciate about Ethereum is decentralization and CROPS. The main pragmatic benefit that these things translate into is stability. SoV is the category where that is not an unneeded extra we merely put effort into for ideological reasons, but rather a pragmatic strength from the perspective of people putting in their assets. And in the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued.

x.name: vitalik.eth
x.text:
# 1. ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed

Let us re-cap the economic theory behind valuation of a fee-burning token. This is the "net present value" (NPV) theory.

Formula: market cap = fees burned / discount rate

Imagine you have a token of which $1 billion is burned per year, and this is a long-term stable equilibrium. Now, imagine the discount rate is 4%; that is, people value having $1B today as much as $1.04B in one year.

The idea is that $1B / 4% = $25B serves as a natural "floor" for the valuation: if the valuation drops lower than that, then someone could buy an asset expected to pay $1 per year forever for less than $25 (by buying some tokens, and then selling >4% of their supply each year so their share of the total pie remains the same), and so by buying the asset you reliably beat the market.

In 2021-23, Ethereum burned millions of ETH per year in this way.

But here's the problem: this was never a true floor. The reason is that the bulk of that burn was crypto-internal use cases. If ETH had dropped by 10x, then the profits from those use cases would have also dropped, because all the buyers would have had much less money to pay with. This applies both to things like that infamous $180m-fees-burned-in-one-day digital monkey sale (yes, this happened; if you don't remember look it up!), and to more "normal" things like lending. The floor argument only works if the backing of the revenue stream is external.

Today, Ethereum actually has a better claim to this external backing, because of the growing RWA economy, but on the other hand, perhaps precisely because it's a normal stable mature business, it's not going to randomly go crazy and burn $180m on a digital monkey sale.

I know this is a predictable opinion from me but I don't agree with the strong emotional reaction against the anti-data-center movements that I've seen this week.

As I see it, algorithmic progress means that whatever you would be able to do with more and bigger data centers in 2 years, you will be able to do with the data centers we have today in 4 years - probably sooner. So nothing remotely apocalyptically bad will happen from even extreme levels of success by anti-data-center people.

Meanwhile we need all the time we can get to better harden the world against both already-visible cybersecurity issues and any bio and other risks soon to come. Science applications are bottlenecked by many things other than AI, so slowing AI down by one year will slow those down by much less than one year.

Given this, a slowdown in compute hyper-scaling seems quite net good? Notice this is without any controversial "doomer arguments", RSI etc. Even if net-bad, it's certainly not worse than like 10+ other political things.

x.name: Bull Theory
x.text:
North Korean hackers are launching MEMECOINS to launder money from the $6.3 Billion Binance hack.

Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic found six such memecoins, created between November 5 and 7, each costing about $90.

The trick is simple. Hackers create a liquidity pool on a DeFi exchange, pairing the memecoin with a real crypto like NEAR.

One hacker wallet buys the memecoin with stolen NEAR, while another sells it back into the same pool for NEAR.

This makes the receiving wallet look like it earned money through normal trading. They’ve already moved $430,000 this way on NEAR, and the same trick has shown up on Tron and Solana.

This makes the stolen crypto harder to trace.

Stolen USDT and USDC can be frozen by their issuers, but BTC, ETH and NEAR are not centrally controlled and can be transferred.

Hackers used this exact process in the 2025 Bybit breach, the largest crypto theft before Binance.

x.name: The Undercurrent
x.text:
I wonder how many Americans actually understand where their federal taxes are going.

The IRS just released the 2027 tax brackets. So I decided to do a little math.

In 2026, the federal government collected $5.4 trillion in revenue and spent $1.05 trillion just paying interest on the national debt.

That’s equivalent to nearly 20% of everything it collected.

Using the new tax brackets, a single person earning $50,000 would owe roughly $3,752 in federal income taxes before credits. About $730 of that is equivalent to the government’s current interest burden.

A married couple earning $150,000? Roughly $2,877.

And what do we get for those interest payments? Nothing new. No roads. No schools. No services. Just the cost of money Washington already borrowed and spent.

In 2016, interest consumed the equivalent of about 7% of federal revenue. Now it’s nearly 20%.

And we’re still borrowing almost $2 trillion a year.

How long do Americans think this can continue?

x.name: WOLF
x.text:
THE IRS JUST RELEASED THE NEW 2027 🇺🇸 TAX BRACKETS. HERE'S HOW THEY WORK IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Every bracket got a little bigger to keep up with inflation, so you can earn a bit more before moving into a higher rate.

Step 1: Take what you earn and subtract the standard deduction. That part isn't taxed at all.
- Single: $16,600
- Married: $33,200

Step 2: Whatever's left gets taxed in layers.

Single filers:
- 10% on your first $12,800
- 12% on income up to $52,025
- 22% up to $109,125
- 24% up to $208,325
- 32% up to $264,550
- 35% up to $661,375
- 37% on anything above that

Married couples: the cutoffs are roughly double ($25,600, $104,050, $218,250, $416,650, $529,100, $793,650).

Example: You're single and earn $76,600. Subtract $16,600 and you're taxed on $60,000.

- 10% on the first $12,800 = $1,280
- 12% on the next $39,225 = $4,707
- 22% on the last $7,975 = $1,755

Total: about $7,742 in federal income tax, or roughly 10% of what you earned.

Even though you're "in" the 22% bracket, only your last $7,975 gets taxed at 22%.

x.name: Nick Huber
x.text:
There are two questions you should be asking about any opportunity you are considering going after:

1. What is the return, in dollars, for an hour of my time today, a year from now, and 10 years from now?

2. If I stop working, do I stop getting paid or will I keep getting paid?

The answers to those questions will tell you all you need to know about the choices you’re making. 

If your goal is wealth and doing what you want to do when you want to do it, you need to consider if your current career path lends itself to getting paid even if you’re not working at some point in the future.

If your answer is no, then it’s time to stop doing what you’re doing and start building the leverage you need to change that.

What I’ve learned is that the amount of money you earn is not correlated to how hard you work it is correlated to how hard you are to replace and thus how much leverage you have.

If you are easy to replace, then you have low leverage and a capped earning potential. But if you are impossible to replace, you have high leverage and unlimited earning potential.

So your goal should be to start a business (or businesses) and get to a point where people need you more than you need them.

x.name: SightBringer
x.text:
⚡️The American upper-middle class has built its financial life around an assumption that is beginning to fail: that professional earning power is a durable asset.

The deeper problem is that a $320,000 salary was never an asset on the household balance sheet. It was a recurring payment from an institution that could terminate the arrangement.

Yet the mortgage, lifestyle, and long-term obligations were structured as though that payment would continue.

Temporary access to institutional income was converted into permanent financial commitments.

For decades, this worked because professional experience generally accumulated value. A manager who lost a job could often sell the same expertise to another company at comparable compensation.

AI is attacking that replacement mechanism.

A company eliminating a management position can now reconsider whether the function requires another manager at all. When enough employers make that calculation simultaneously, displaced professionals discover that their previous compensation was supported by an organizational structure that is being dismantled.

And the most consequential part is the asymmetry.

A company can reduce its labor costs immediately. A household cannot reduce its financial obligations at the same speed.

That creates forced adaptation. Savings disappear. Assets get liquidated. Housing decisions change. Families that appeared wealthy discover how much of their security depended on uninterrupted employment.

The next phase of white-collar displacement will expose a distinction that high salaries concealed for decades.

Many Americans who appeared financially successful were actually highly compensated participants in a system they did not control.

Their standard of living was substantial. Their independence was fragile.

And the emerging economy is beginning to price those two things very differently.

The deepest signal is that the economic value of professional labor is becoming less durable precisely as the financial commitments built upon that labor have become larger.

That is the transmission mechanism from AI productivity to household financial distress.

And it has only begun.

올해 내내 기우제지내듯 적어왔던

그런데,
닷컴버블을 겪어보진 못했지만
당시 시장상황들을 책으로 읽어보고,

제가 직접 겪었던 2017년 코인 ICO광풍때의 모습을 떠올려보아도

이번 AI발 상승은
무실적 잡주/잡코인이 무더기로 상장하며 설거지를 하던 위 사례들과는 달리

제대로된 회사들과 실적을 바탕으로 상승한거같은데 말입니다...

닷컴버블 당시나
2017년의 코인시장처럼 광기로 밀어올리던
블로우오프탑의 형태도 아닌거같고...

만약 25년의 상승을 마무리 짓고 진짜 본격적인 조정의 시작이라면 이걸로는 안 끝날텐데.

정말 헷갈리네요.

일단 AI에게 같은 질문을 해본바
답변 :

버블의 두 가지 유형: 
'개미 주도 투기 버블' vs '자본 지출(Capex) 과잉 버블'

우리가 기억하는 1999년 닷컴버블이나 2017년 ICO 열풍은 '개미 주도의 밸류에이션 부재 투기 버블'이었습니다. 실적 없는 껍데기 회사에 돈이 몰렸기 때문에 꼭대기에서 수직으로 솟구치는 '블로우오프 탑(Blow-off Top)' 캔들이 나왔습니다.

하지만 자본주의 역사에는 또 다른 형태의 치명적인 버블이 존재합니다. 바로 1840년대 영국의 철도 광풍(Railway Mania)이나 1929년 대공황 직전의 전력/제조업 버블, 그리고 1990년대 시스코(Cisco)의 광케이블 버블입니다.

실적 기반 버블의 치명적인 함정:

1999년 당시 통신 장비 1위였던 시스코(Cisco)는 적자 기업이 아니었습니다. 전 세계 인터넷 인프라를 깔기 위해 통신사들이 너도나도 시스코 라우터를 사들이면서 분기마다 역대급 실적과 어닝 서프라이즈를 냈습니다.

엔비디아, TSMC, SK하이닉스 역시 마찬가지입니다. 이들의 실적이 뛰어난 이유는 기술이 가짜여서가 아니라, 마이크로소프트, 구글, 메타, 아마존 등 빅테크들이 "AI 패권을 뺏기면 끝장"이라는 공포(FOMO) 때문에 천문학적인 잉여현금(Capex)을 엔비디아 칩 구매와 데이터센터에 쏟아부었기 때문입니다.

버블의 본질은 '최종 소비자의 수익성(ROI)':

칩 제조사는 돈을 엄청나게 벌었지만(실적 장세), 정작 그 칩을 수천억 달러어치 사들인 빅테크와 네오클라우드들은 AI 소프트웨어 서비스에서 그만큼의 매출을 뽑아내지 못하고 있습니다.

신규 데이터센터를 짓던 네오클라우드들의 CDS 프리미엄이 치솟고 B300 GPU 렌탈비가 폭락하는 현상이 바로 이를 증명합니다.   

즉, 이번 버블은 '사기 기업의 난립'이 아니라 '우량 기업들이 빚과 현금을 털어 미래 수요를 너무 앞당겨 투자해 버린 자본 과잉(Capex 과잉) 버블'입니다.

머니플로우 ’26.11.4

코스피: 5,500깨고 주저 앉을게
전자닉스: 아침에 띄운 갭까지 다 토할게
심텍, 코리아써키트: 우린 그래도 빨간불 켤게
일본 반도체: 휴장 복귀 후 밀린 매 맞을게
한진칼: 일반 개미 못타게 요란하게 운전할게
태양광: 중간선거 민주당 승리에 베팅할게

간밤 나스닥 0.8%, SOX 2.6%로 반도체가 앞서서 반등.
메모리 비메모리 가리지 않고 대부분 반등하며 분위기 띄움.
AMD는 매출 QoQ 가이던스 27% 제시하며 시간외 7% 상승.
밤 사이에 이란과 대화 물꼬도 트이는거 같으며 미장 반등.

문제는 정규장 열고나서 나스닥 선물이 방향을 틀어버렸음.
프리마켓서 0.6% 오르던 나선이 지금은 -1.8%까지 꼬라박음
미국 중간선거 개표초반부터 민주당이 경합주에서 앞서버림.
노스캐롤라이나 상원 의석도 가져감. 양원 다수당 승리는 아직

코스피는 2.4% 갭상승 후 5,828까지 찍고 장중고가 3.17%.
지금은 -3%까지 빠지면서 5,500선도 그냥 깨고 주저앉음.
최근까지 청기백기 오르고내리더니 오늘은 그냥 아래로 박살.
코스닥도 2%까지 올랐다가 -2.5%까지 같이 끌려내려 옴.

코스피 하락종목은 상승의 4배, 코스닥은 4.5배에 달하는 중.
외국인은 코스피에서 벌써 1.5조원 넘게 순매도하는 중.
선물은 외인 기관 모두 양매수지만 꼴랑 몇백억 수준.

삼성전자, SK하이닉스는 프리마켓에서 3%, 4%대 상승.
정규장들어와선 -3.4%, -5.1%로 자중고점에서 6~9% 빠짐
효성중공업, 삼성SDI도 프리마켓 상승분 다 뱉고 하락 전환.

그 와중 심텍과 코리아써키트는 9% 가량 상승하며 버티는중
지수가 이 지경인데 이렇게 버티는걸 보면 얘네도 보통 아님.
심텍은 어제 컨센 20% 상회 후 기판 수요 대응 증설까지 발표.
마침 새벽에 AMD가 본인들 칩 수요 좋다고 실적발표한 덕분.

한국만 이러는게 아님. 어제 쉬었던 니케이도 -3.6% 밀렸음.
키옥시아 -12%, 어드반테스트 -8%. 도쿄일렉트론 -6.5%
한일 모두 반도체 관련주들이 깨지는건 매한가지인 상황. 
일본 기판주 이비덴 -7%인데 한국 기판들 버티는게 용하다.

한진칼 지분 싸움 덕 8%대 상승. 근데 기사님 운전이 요란함.
프리마켓 15% 상승, 정규장 -7.5% 하락 후 저점대비 17% 반등
기사 운전하는 꼬라지보니 어지간한 개미들 그냥 안태워줄듯.

최근 머니플로우, 클로징코멘트에서 계속 얘기했듯이 관망중.
중간선거 관련 변동성이 커질 수 밖에 없다는건 계속 얘기했음
오늘 반등했다하더라도 상승 유지 가능성이 높지않았을 것임.
반대로 오늘 빠진다해도 많이빠졌으니 반등도 강할 수도 있음.

변동성이 크다는건 위든 아래든 요란하게 움직인다는 소리임.
이 방향성 예측이 어려운 구간이니 이런 구간에선 그냥 관망.
아래든 위든 추세가 확인된 뒤에 매매하는게 낫다는게 내 생각

누차 말하지만 난 '존버' 혹은 '버텨라'라고 말한적이 없음.
어려운구간 지나가면 반등이 온다는게 존버하란 소리가 아님.
많이 오르면 빠지고, 많이 빠지면 반등하고 순환 한단것뿐임.

국장 욕하고 미장 갔던 사람들은 환율, 주가 양빵으로 터짐.
그렇다고 코인 간 사람들은 해킹 여파로 허우적대고 있음. 
도망친 곳에 낙원은 없음. 위험자산이 전반적으로 약한것뿐임.

The AI selloff has become so severe that Taiwan is now restricting short selling and preparing a $15 BILLION emergency fund to support its stock market.

Companies are also being encouraged to buy back their own shares.

Taiwan is one of the most important countries in the global semiconductor supply chain.

• Diesel: Maximum 50 litres.

And this is happening while rising oil prices are already pushing inflation higher in many countries.

Higher fuel prices also mean higher transportation, food and manufacturing costs.

With the Iran war already disrupting global energy supplies, further cuts to Russian fuel exports could push diesel prices even higher and make inflation much harder to control.

🚨 Something is seriously wrong with banking security right now.

In just a few weeks, banks and financial institutions across six countries have reported stolen funds, major security breaches and system failures.

And some of these incidents are genuinely alarming.

France: Hackers stole approximately $112 MILLION from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, a bank serving more than 5.8 MILLION customers.

They reportedly gained access through an outside service provider and transferred the money using the bank's own account.

The attack was so serious that French prosecutors opened a criminal investigation.

Taiwan: Hackers exploited security settings in Bank SinoPac's mobile banking system and made 427 unauthorized transfers worth $1.3 MILLION.

Around 419 customer accounts were affected, with the money sent to a single account at another bank.

South Korea: Authorities reported 40 security incidents across 37 financial companies in just over a month.

Approximately 473,000 personal information records were exposed, while around $745,000 was stolen.

Regulators are now ordering security checks at 580 financial companies.

But the problems didn't stop there.

Japan: A single equipment failure disrupted banking services at 128 credit unions on November 6.

Customers suddenly couldn't withdraw cash from ATMs, make deposits or complete normal banking transactions.

The failure affected more than HALF of Japan's 236 credit unions before services were restored later that day.

Malaysia: Bank Rakyat's website was defaced, while two other banks reported separate service disruptions.

Authorities say customer deposits and core banking systems were not compromised.

Indonesia: A cybersecurity monitoring system recorded more than 200,000 suspected attack activities targeting banking, finance and insurance in a 24-hour period.

These were detected threats, not confirmed successful breaches.

And there's another development.

According to Reuters, the Federal Reserve and U.S. banking regulators contacted banks after the reported $6.3 BILLION Binance hack, checking for unusual activity and possible security weaknesses.

Just look at the scale of what's happening.

In France, attackers allegedly used a trusted outside provider to steal more than $100 million.

In Taiwan, a weakness in a banking app's security settings allowed hundreds of unauthorized transfers.

And in Japan, a single technical failure temporarily disrupted banking services at 128 institutions.

These incidents have different causes, but they expose a serious weakness in modern banking.

Banks depend on outside technology providers, shared payment networks and software systems that millions of customers use every day.

If one failure can temporarily shut down 128 credit unions, imagine the disruption a successful attack on a major shared banking network could cause.

🚨 The entire U.S. financial system is becoming dangerously dependent on AI.

And the numbers are much worse than most people realize.

According to a Bloomberg analysis, AI has become so deeply connected to the U.S. stock market, pension funds, corporate debt and economic growth that a serious downturn could affect almost everyone.

Here's how big this has become.

1. The stock market

Since ChatGPT launched in November 2022, the S&P 500 added nearly $32 TRILLION in market value through November 3.

More than HALF of those gains came from just 10 companies, all connected to AI.

Technology and tech-related companies now account for nearly 50% of the S&P 500's value, even more than during the dot-com bubble.

Nvidia alone recently represented around 8% of the entire index.

This means a crash in a handful of AI companies could drag down the broader stock market, even if other businesses are performing well.

2. Retirement savings

The risk isn't limited to people buying AI stocks.

Bloomberg analyzed more than 70 U.S. pension funds and found that around 44% of their stock investments, worth $610 BILLION, are now tied to technology.

Hedge funds and insurance companies have also increased their exposure.

So even people who have never bought Nvidia, Microsoft or other AI stocks could be affected through their retirement savings.

3. The massive debt problem

This is probably the most concerning part.

Technology companies issued $296 BILLION in investment-grade bonds through October 12, making tech the largest nonfinancial borrowing sector.

Meanwhile, AI infrastructure developers issued more than $43 BILLION in high-yield debt, compared with just $8.5 billion last year.

Technology's share of the junk-bond market has nearly tripled to 19.7%.

And the six biggest cloud companies are expected to spend more than $850 BILLION this year on AI-related projects.

That's an 83% increase from 2025.

The concern is that companies are taking on enormous financial commitments today based on profits they expect to earn years from now.

If those profits disappoint, the damage won't be limited to shareholders.

Banks, bondholders and investment firms financing these projects could suffer losses too.

4. The U.S. economy

AI-related investment has become one of the biggest drivers of American economic growth.

Spending on technology hardware, software and data centers now makes up more than one-third of all U.S. business investment.

And these categories accounted for most of the growth in business investment over the past year.

So if companies suddenly cut AI spending, it could affect construction, electricity demand, equipment suppliers, jobs and overall economic growth.

That's why the recent AI stock selloff is so important.

The U.S. economy has become increasingly dependent on companies continuing to spend hundreds of billions building AI infrastructure.

But there's still a major unanswered question.

Can AI companies eventually generate enough profits to justify all this investment?

Because right now, the same industry is supporting stock valuations, retirement portfolios, corporate borrowing and a significant part of economic growth.

If the AI boom suffers a prolonged collapse, this won't just be another tech stock crash. The consequences could spread across the entire U.S. financial system.

x.name: 아하도
x.text:
주말에 과거차트 말고 현재 미래차트보고 있다가
생각나는 대로 적어보겠습니다

일단 이 글을 적으면 꼭 한두분은 오해하시는 분들이 있어서
앞서서 글을 적자면 저는 연말까지 상승뷰 입니다

지금 이 가정은 내 상승뷰를 지우고
그냥 하락한다고 보았을때 나타날수 있는 경우의 수를 보는 것입니다

1. 월봉 
하락을 시작했으면 그 다음 선을 찍으러 보통 옵니다
20월선을 하회해서 그 다음인 60월선을 가려면 최소 1년짜리 하락장이란 소리입니다. 당연히 그 중간중간에 월봉상 양봉도 나와야 하고요. 거기까지 간다고 생각하는 분들은 아무도 없을테니
우리는 20월선 즈음에서 하락을 마무리한다고 합의를 보겠습니다

방법은 약 3개입니다
찍고 오르거나 긴 밑꼬리를 남기거나
아니면 음봉을 남기고 다음달에 양봉으로 오르거나

일단 3번이 되려면 지금 11월이 3주나 남았는데 
시간이 너무 많이 남았기 때문에 확률상 위의 두개가 더 높다고 보겠습니다

그러면 어느쪽도 11월 안에 하락이 끝난다는 뜻이 됩니다
물론 같은 자리를 월봉상 또 내려올수는 있는데
그럴려면 어차피 월초에 많이 올렸다가 내려야 하니까
그건 일단 논외로하고

2. 주봉
일봉상 지지선이 없기 때문에
일봉으로 내릴거면 주봉에 어딘가 닿기 위해 내려야 합니다
만약 여기서 더 내릴거라면
그 다음주봉인 qqq 585까지 내린단 소리가 됩니다

중간에 610까지 한 2-3주간 내렸다가 올라갈수 없냐고요?
그런식으로 일봉과 주봉이 둘다 애매한곳까지 아무것도 닿지않고 조정이 끝나지는 않습니다

현재 닿은 주봉상 60선을 이탈할거라면 그 다음 도착지는 이미 정해져 있는 것입니다

그러면 내려가는 방법은 두개 입니다
5일선을 타고 몇주에 걸쳐 내려가던가
1-2주 안에 한꺼번에 내리던가

근데 전자는 이미 월봉때문제 가능한 옵션이 아니기 때문에 내릴거라면 후자밖에 남지 않습니다
그런데 이걸 할거라면 1-2주간의 애매한 상승이 나올겁니다
지금 이 자리에서 바로 내려가기는 힘들기 때문에
한 200일선까지 닿으러 가는. 그래서 제가 애매한 상승이 나오면 비중조절을 하겠다고 한것입니다

3. 일봉
일봉은 이미 200일선을 하회했고
밑에 선이 없어서 내리려면 5일선을 밟고 내려야 합니다
그런데 이미 중간에 거래량도 많은 파이널 하락같은 장대음봉이 있습니다. 그 음봉을 두고 585까지 5일선을 타고 1프로씩 몇주간 내린다?
저는 그런 그림을 일단 본적이 없습니다

x.name: The Kobeissi Letter
x.text:
The scale of Big Tech's AI future financial obligations is extraordinary:

Alphabet, $GOOGL, Meta, $META, Anthropic, Microsoft, $MSFT, Amazon, $AMZN, Oracle, $ORCL, and Nvidia, $NVDA, have disclosed a combined $4.49 trillion in off-balance-sheet obligations.

These include future lease payments that have not yet commenced, data-center commitments, equipment purchases, and other contractual obligations.

Alphabet accounts for the largest amount, at $1.08 trillion, followed by Anthropic, at $865 billion, and Meta, at $810 billion.

By comparison, their combined on-balance-sheet obligations total just $758 billion, consisting of long-term debt and existing lease liabilities.

This means off-balance-sheet commitments are nearly 6 times larger than their on-balance-sheet obligations.

In total, these 7 tech companies face ~$5.25 trillion in combined financial obligations.

The AI infrastructure race is facing enormous future financial commitments.

x.name: Noah' Ark
x.text:
"XRP looks like a scam, and XRP needs to collapse for many people to lose money."

원작 동화 및 영화 《오즈의 마법사》(The Wonderful Wizard of Oz)에서 '사기꾼 마법사'의 정체는 에메랄드 시티의 지배자로 행세하던 '오즈(The Wizard of Oz)'입니다.
• 실체: 그는 마법 능력이 전혀 없는 평범한 캔자스주 오마하 출신의 서커스단 기구 조종사이자 환상술사입니다.
• 정체 발각: 열기구를 타고 바람에 날려 오즈의 나라에 떨어진 뒤, 거대한 환영과 불꽃을 이용해 위대한 마법사인 척 군림했으나 도로시와 일행이 커튼 뒤의 진짜 모습을 발견하면서 사기임이 밝혀집니다.
• 결말: 진짜 마법은 쓰지 못했지만, 허수아비에게 뇌 모양의 상징물을 주고 사자에게 용기 증서를 주는 등 심리적인 속임수와 지혜로 일행의 소원을 이루어주었고, 이후 다시 열기구를 타고 캔자스로 떠납니다.

쥬라기공원에 출연했던 Rockstar 제프 골드블럼(Jeff Goldblum)은 영화 위키드 (2024)와 속편 위키드: 포 굿 (2025)에서 사기꾼(scam) 마법사 역할을 맡았습니다.
극 중 제프 골드블럼이 연기한 오즈의 마법사는 실제로는 아무런 초자연적 마법 능력이 없지만, 기계 장치와 속임수(트릭)를 이용해 위대한 마법사 행세를 하며 오즈를 통치하는 인물입니다.
• 원작 및 세계관: 오마하에서 열기구를 타고 표류해 온 평범한 인간으로, 시민들을 속여 권력을 유지한다는 설정은 원작 소설 《오즈의 마법사》에서 이어진 캐릭터의 본질입니다.
• 주요 연기 특징: 유튜브 인터뷰 영상에 따르면, 제프 골드블럼은 실제 마술 트릭(동전 마술 등)을 연습해 캐릭터가 초능력자가 아닌 일종의 눈속임 마술사라는 점을 표현했습니다.

동전마술(Coin Magic)은 동전을 이용해 관객 눈앞에서 동전이 사라지거나 나타나고, 순간이동하거나 변하는 것처럼 보이게 하는 클로즈업 마술의 한 분야입니다.
주변에서 쉽게 구할 수 있는 소품을 활용하기 때문에 별도의 무대 장치 없이도 관객과 아주 가까운 거리에서 즉흥적으로 선보일 수 있습니다.
• 핵심 원리: 마법 같은 초능력이 아니라, 정교한 손기술(슬라이트 오브 핸드)과 관객의 시선을 다른 곳으로 유도하는 심리적 기법(미스디렉션)을 결합해 착시를 일으킵니다.
• 대표적인 기초 기술: 손바닥 근육이나 손가락 사이에 동전을 감추어 빈손처럼 보이게 하는 팜(Palm)과, 동전을 다른 손에 옮겨 쥔 것처럼 속이는 프렌치 드롭(French Drop) 등이 있습니다.
• 주요 연출 효과: 동전 여러 개가 한곳으로 모이는 '매트릭스', 유리컵이나 탁자를 통과하는 '관통 마술', 동전의 크기나 종류가 바뀌는 '체인지' 등이 대표적입니다.

1. 상장 직후의 주가 폭락 (프리미엄의 붕괴)

마이크로스트래티지처럼 공격적으로 XRP를 매집하겠다며 나스닥에 입성한 에버노스지만, 현실은 냉혹했습니다.

상장 직후 19달러 선을 터치했던 주가는 불과 단기간에 11.70달러까지 약 44~45% 폭락하며 역사적 신저가를 기록했습니다.

2. RLUSD 통계의 착시 현상 (데이터의 함정)

에버노스 측은 "XRPL 자체 탈중앙화 거래소(DEX)에서 이뤄진 RLUSD 교환 거래의 92%에 XRP가 사용되었다"며 긍정적인 수치를 발표했습니다.

하지만 이는 전체 글로벌 RLUSD 유통 거래량이 아닌, 오직 '자체 DEX'에만 한정된 통계입니다.

착시 효과를 노린 과도한 통계적 낙관론을 철저히 경계해야 할 시점입니다.

3. 자금 조달 난항과 최악의 'XRP 매도' 리스크

가장 치명적인 뇌관은 회사의 현금 흐름과 부채입니다.

주가 하락이 지속되어 시장에서의 자금 조달에 난항을 겪을 경우, 에버노스는 약 3천만 달러 규모의 부채 상환이나 운영 재원을 마련하기 위해 자신들이 모아둔 4억 7,300만 개의 XRP 리저브를 헐값에 시장에 내다 팔아야 하는 최악의 딜레마에 빠질 수 있습니다.

💡 비트코인과 마이크로스트래티지의 성공 방정식을 XRP 생태계에 맹목적으로 대입하기엔 아직 펀더멘털과 시장 환경의 차이가 큽니다.

 '기관이 자산을 매집한다'는 표면적인 호재성 내러티브에만 열광할 것이 아니라, 그들이 내세우는 통계의 허점을 간파하고 악화되는 현금 흐름 속에서 잠재적 매도 물량으로 돌변할 리스크를 냉정하게 계산해야 합니다.

거시적 트레저리 모델 관점에서 볼 때, 기업이 신주를 발행해 코인을 사는 이른바 '프리미엄 밸브' 시스템은 기업의 주가가 보유 자산 가치보다 고평가될 때만 선순환을 일으킵니다.

에버노스의 주가가 지속적으로 하락하여 자본 조달 창구가 막히면 이 사이클은 완전히 붕괴합니다.

오히려 기업의 생존을 위해 거대한 XRP 금고가 강제 청산되며 막대한 매도 압력을 만들어내는 유동성 리스크의 진원지가 될 확률이 있을 수도 있습니다.

결론적으로, 'XRP 생태계의 든든한 금고'가 될 줄 알았던 에버노스가 시장의 변동성을 키우는 뇌관이 될 수 있음도 인지는 하고 있어야 합니다.

x.name: Bit Safe Zone
x.text:
[왜 한국인은 리플을 좋아할까? 뇌피셜 버전]

- 저는 2017년 10월쯤 빗썸에 가입하면서 코인 투자를 처음 시작했습니다. 업비트가 오픈하기 직전이라, 사실상 빗썸이 국내 대표 거래소였던 시절입니다.

- 지금과 달리 당시 빗썸에 상장된 코인은 10개 남짓에 불과했습니다. 비트코인, 이더리움, 이더리움 클래식, 라이트코인, 그리고 리플 정도가 주로 거래되던 코인이었죠.

- 그 중 리플은 225원 안팎으로, 다른 코인에 비해 압도적으로 저렴했습니다. 참고로 이더리움이 33만 7천 원에 닿기만 하면 떨어진다고 ‘337 박수'로 조롱받던 시절이였습니다.

- 10만 원으로 비트코인을 사봐야 수량이 눈에 띄지도 않았지만, 리플은 달랐습니다. 10만 원이면 수백 개를 살 수 있었거든요. 그래서 이런 생각이 들었습니다. "비트코인도 1달러 시절이 있었는데 지금은 수백만 원이잖아. 리플도 가능하지 않을까? 하다못해 라이트코인 가격만 가줘도 수백 배인데."

- 지금 생각하면 발행량을 고려하지 않은 전형적인 착각이였습니다. 리플은 발행량이 1,000억 개에 달해서, 단위 가격이 싼 것과 저평가된 것은 전혀 다른 이야기였죠. 하지만 당시 저 같은 초보 투자자에게 '싼 가격'과 '많은 개수'는 무엇보다 강력한 매력이었습니다.

- 그렇게 돈이 생기는 대로 리플을 사 모으기 시작했고, 몇 달 뒤 모두가 아는 2017년 말 대폭등장이 찾아왔습니다. 리플은 국내 거래소 기준 4,900원 안팎까지 치솟았습니다. 저는 400~500원에 이미 다 팔아버려서 배만 아팠죠.

- 문제는 그다음입니다. 폭등 소식을 듣고 고점 근처에서 뛰어든 사람들이 정말 많았습니다. 소액으로 '대박'을 노릴 수 있는 코인은 사실상 리플이었고, 김치 프리미엄까지 붙어 국내 고점은 해외보다도 높았습니다.

- 이후 대폭락장이 오면서 리플은 다시 400원대까지 내려왔습니다. 떨어지는 와중에 물린 홀더들은 물타기를 거듭하며 '존버'에 들어갔습니다.

- 결과적으로 이미 쏟아부은 돈과 기다린 세월이 아까워서, 즉 매몰비용 때문에 쉽게 팔지 못하고 버티게 된 겁니다. 그렇게 오랜 시간을 함께 버틴 홀더들 사이에서는 단순한 투자를 넘어선 애착과 결속이 생겼고, 이것이 지금까지 이어지는 "한국인의 리플 사랑"의 뿌리가 아닐까 생각합니다.
